# Clostridioides difficile infection

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Clostridioides difficile infection*

[Original Article Link](/library/dS0oA2)

---

## Summary

<u>Clostridioides difficile</u> (<u>C. difficile</u>; formerly known as <u>Clostridium difficile</u>) is a gram-positive <u>bacillus</u> that can cause <u>antibiotic</u>-associated <u>diarrhea</u>. Rates of <u>C. difficile</u> infection (<u>CDI</u>) are particularly high among hospitalized patients and residents in long-term care facilities because <u>C. difficile</u> spores are easily transmitted (<u>fecal-oral route</u>) and difficult to eradicate. The bacterium is resistant to multiple <u>antibiotics</u>, and <u>colonization</u> with <u>C. difficile</u> most commonly occurs following <u>antibiotic</u> treatment for other diseases. The resulting damage to the intestinal flora promotes <u>C. difficile</u> infection, which typically manifests with <u>diarrhea</u> accompanied by <u>fever</u> and abdominal <u>pain</u>. <u>Severe CDI</u> or <u>fulminant CDI</u> may manifest with <u>paralytic ileus</u> or <u>toxic megacolon</u>. In most cases, however, <u>colonization</u> results in asymptomatic carriage. Diagnosis of symptomatic patients is based on <u>stool tests for CDI</u>, which detect toxins or toxigenic strains of <u>C. difficile</u> or the identification of <u>pseudomembranous colitis</u> on imaging or endoscopy. <u>Vancomycin</u> and <u>fidaxomicin</u> are the preferred <u>antibiotic</u> agents for treating <u>CDI</u>. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, measures to prevent transmission (e.g., <u>patient cohorting</u> or isolation, strict adherence to hygiene measures) should be followed, especially in hospitals and other health care settings.

---

## Etiology

### Causative <u>pathogen</u>: <u>Clostridioides difficile</u>




* Gram-positive <u>bacillus</u>, <u>obligate anaerobe</u>

* Can be toxigenic or non-toxigenic; toxigenic strains cause <u>C. difficile</u> infection (<u>CDI</u>)

* Forms environmentally-resistant spores (capable of withstanding heat, <u>antibiotics</u>, and acid)

* Germination of spores turns them into functional <u>bacilli</u>

* Highly contagious

* Present ubiquitously

* Oral route of transmission

* <u>Community-acquired CDI</u>: <u>fecal-oral route</u>

* <u>Hospital-acquired CDI</u>: via contaminated surfaces and medical equipment





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>C. difficile</u> strain must be toxigenic to cause the disease. Intestinal <u>colonization</u> by nontoxigenic strains will result in asymptomatic carriage.




### Risk factors for CDI [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[6]](/library/wRXh6B)




* Recent <u>antibiotic</u> treatment ;  [[7]](/library/vO0A8T)[[8]](/library/KJbUEu) 

* High-risk <u>antibiotics</u> (<u>odds ratio</u> ≥ 5)

* <u>Clindamycin</u>

* <u>Cephalosporins</u>

* <u>Fluoroquinolones</u>

* Moderate risk <u>antibiotics</u> (<u>odds ratio</u> 1 to 5)

* <u>Penicillin</u>

* <u>Macrolides</u>

* Advanced age

* <u>Gastric acid</u> suppression (e.g., with <u>proton pump inhibitors</u>) or bypass (e.g., <u>enteral feeding</u>)

* Recent hospitalization

* Severe illnesses

* Immune suppression

* <u>Inflammatory bowel disease</u> [[9]](/library/9RXN6B)

---

## Pathophysiology

<u>C. difficile</u> possesses a range of <u>virulence factors</u>, the most important of which are toxins A and B. [[10]](/library/ppYLqJ)[[11]](/library/JpYsqJ)




### Toxin A (<u>enterotoxin</u>)




* Structure

* <u>Active site</u> at N-terminal domain

* Central hydrophobic domain

* Binding site at C-terminal domain

* Mechanism of action: binding to brush border of <u>enterocytes</u>:  → <u>receptor</u>-mediated <u>endocytosis</u> → change of conformation → exposure of active domain → <u>glycosylation</u> of target <u>proteins</u> (e.g., Rac, Cdc42, RhoA) → disruption of <u>actin</u> <u>cytoskeleton</u> functioning → increase in <u>epithelial</u> permeability and <u>apoptosis</u> → <u>diarrhea</u>





### Toxin B (cytotoxin)




* Structure

* Binding site at C-terminal domain

* Translocation domain

* <u>Cysteine</u> <u>protease</u>-containing domain

* Catalytic domain

* Mechanism of action: same as in <u>toxin A</u>, but can also cause pore formation within the endosomal membrane via insertion of the translocation domain → release of endosomal content into the <u>cytosol</u> → cytopathic effect

---

## Clinical features

Symptoms typically develop during <u>antibiotic</u> treatment or 2–10 days following its initiation; however, 25–40% of cases manifest as late as 10 weeks following treatment.




* <u>Watery diarrhea</u> (<u>C. difficile</u>-associated <u>diarrhea</u> or CDAD)

* ≥ 3 stools per day associated with a characteristic odor

* May contain traces of mucus or occult blood

* <u>Hematochezia</u> and <u>melena</u> are both rare.

* Cramping abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>anorexia</u>

* Abdominal tenderness

* <u>Fever</u> and <u>dehydration</u> (especially in severe cases)

* <u>Fulminant CDI</u> may manifest with abdominal distention and severe <u>hypovolemia</u> (e.g., due to <u>toxic megacolon</u>, <u>paralytic ileus</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> Clostridioides difficile Causes Difficult Diarrhea.




References:[[12]](/library/CO0quT)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




* The diagnosis of <u>CDI</u> is based on the presence of typical clinical features (especially in patients with <u>risk factors for CDI</u>) and either of the following:

* <u>C. difficile</u> toxins or toxigenic strains of C.difficile detected on <u>stool tests for CDI</u>

* <u>Pseudomembranous colitis</u> confirmed on endoscopy or <u>histopathology</u>

* Initiate measures to prevent and control the spread of infection (see “<u>Secondary prevention of CDI</u>”).

* Patients with <u>diarrhea</u>

* Consider other etiologies for <u>diarrhea</u> : See “<u>Diagnostic workup of diarrhea</u>.”

* Suspect <u>CDI</u> in patients with unexplained new-onset <u>diarrhea</u>, especially those with <u>risk factors for CDI</u>.

* Initial tests: stool analysis for toxins and toxigenic strains of <u>C. difficile</u>

* Patients with <u>ileus</u> due to suspected <u>CDI</u>: Consider <u>PCR</u> of rectal swabs.

* Imaging is useful to evaluate undifferentiated abdominal <u>pain</u> or if there is a concern for complications.

* Consider endoscopy if the diagnosis remains uncertain after initial tests or if there is insufficient response to empiric <u>antibiotic therapy for CDI</u>.

* Assess the <u>severity of CDI</u> and initiate <u>antibiotic therapy</u> empirically in patients with <u>fulminant CDI</u>.

* Consult gastroenterology and/or infectious diseases if the diagnosis is unclear.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Patient history</u> and clinical presentation can provide strong indicators for infection, which should be confirmed by stool studies, <u>colonoscopy</u>, or <u>histopathology</u> findings. [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)




### Routine <u>laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)[[13]](/library/2WcTkY0)




Findings are nonspecific and may include the following. [[13]](/library/2WcTkY0)




* <u>CBC</u>: : <u>leukocytosis</u> [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)

* <u>BMP</u>

* ↑ Serum <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalance, particularly <u>hypokalemia</u>

* ↓ Serum <u>albumin</u>

* Blood gases (venous or arterial): ↑ <u>lactate</u>, <u>acidosis</u>





### Stool tests for toxins and toxigenic strains of C. difficile [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




#### Indications




* Adults: unexplained, new-onset loose stools ≥ 3 times in 24 hours

* Children : Consider stool tests in children with prolonged or worsening <u>diarrhea</u>, especially those with <u>risk factors for CDI</u>.





#### Modalities




* Tests with high <u>sensitivity</u> 

* <u>Enzyme immunoassay</u> (<u>EIA</u>) for <u>C. difficile</u> <u>glutamate dehydrogenase</u> <u>antigen</u> (<u>GDH</u>)

* <u>NAAT</u> (e.g., <u>PCR</u>) for <u>C. difficile</u> toxins

* Tests with high <u>specificity</u>: <u>EIA</u> for <u>C. difficile</u> toxins A and B

* Other available tests 

* Cytotoxicity neutralization assay (<u>CCNA</u>): detects toxin in stool

* Culture of toxigenic strains of <u>C. difficile</u>





#### Suggested testing strategy  [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




Consider a multi-test algorithmic approach guided by the <u>pretest probability</u> (<u>PTP</u>) of <u>CDI</u>.




* The initial test should preferably be a high <u>sensitivity</u> test (i.e., <u>NAAT</u> or <u>EIA</u> for <u>GDH</u>).

* Negative <u>NAAT</u> or <u>EIA</u> for <u>GDH</u>: <u>CDI</u> is ruled out.

* Positive <u>NAAT</u> or <u>EIA</u> for <u>GDH</u>: Confirm <u>CDI</u> using a highly specific test, such as <u>EIA</u> for <u>C. difficile</u> toxins 

* Positive <u>EIA</u> for <u>C. difficile</u> toxins: Diagnosis is confirmed.

* Negative <u>EIA</u> for <u>C. difficile</u> toxins 

* High <u>PTP</u> for <u>CDI</u>

* Consider <u>NAAT</u> if not already performed as the initial test.

* Consider empirical <u>antibiotic therapy for CDI</u>.

* Low or moderate <u>PTP</u> for <u>CDI</u>: Consider alternative diagnoses.





> [!TIP]
> Repeat testing within 7 days of <u>diarrhea</u> is not recommended, and asymptomatic individuals should not be tested. [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




### Additional diagnostics




#### Imaging [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[13]](/library/2WcTkY0)




* Indications (not routinely required to diagnose <u>CDI</u>)

* Suspected complications of <u>CDI</u> (e.g., <u>bowel perforation</u>, <u>toxic megacolon</u>, <u>ileus</u>)

* To assess for <u>severity of CDI</u>

* Initial workup of undifferentiated abdominal <u>pain</u> or distension

* Modalities: <u>x-ray abdomen</u> or CT abdomen (with IV and PO contrast)

* Findings [[14]](/library/khcmVX0)[[15]](/library/becHxY0)

* Signs of <u>pseudomembranous colitis</u>, which includes pronounced <u>colonic</u> wall thickening (most common sign) associated with any of the following:

* Accordion sign (on <u>contrast-enhanced CT</u>): alternating areas of low attenuation (due to <u>edematous</u> <u>haustra</u>) and high attenuation (due to contrast material trapped between the thickened <u>haustral folds</u>)

* <u>Colonic</u> wall nodularity

* Pericolonic stranding

* <u>Ascites</u>

* Signs of complications, such as:

* <u>Bowel perforation</u>: <u>free intraperitoneal air</u>

* <u>Toxic megacolon</u>: dilated <u>colon</u> (<u>transverse colon</u> diameter > 6 cm) with loss of haustration

* <u>Paralytic ileus</u>: dilated small and large bowel with no evidence of mechanical obstruction

#### Endoscopy [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[13]](/library/2WcTkY0)




* Indication (not routinely required)

* Consider if the diagnosis remains unclear after initial tests.

* Consider if the <u>PTP</u> of <u>CDI</u> remains high in patients with insufficient response to empirical <u>antibiotic therapy for CDI</u>.

* Modalities: <u>colonoscopy</u> or <u>sigmoidoscopy</u>

* Findings

* <u>Mucosa</u> may appear normal or <u>erythematous</u> and <u>friable</u>.

* Possible signs of pseudomembranous colitis 

* Elevated yellow-white <u>plaques</u> that form pseudomembranes over the <u>colonic</u> <u>mucosa</u>

* May be solitary; widespread; , confluent lesions are seen in severe disease





![Pseudomembranous colitis](media/hee2bxpp9j60axa4ogrsbw86.jpg)

Pseudomembranous colitis

![Pseudomembranous colitis](media/xwh03yudrw5u954x74x0q4zw.jpg)

Pseudomembranous colitis




> [!WARNING]
> Endoscopy may not detect cases of <u>nonsevere CDI</u>, in which pseudomembranes may be absent. [[13]](/library/2WcTkY0)

## Severity classification

The <u>severity of CDI</u> is based on <u>laboratory studies</u> and clinical features and is used to guide disposition, management, and prognosis.




* Nonsevere CDI: <u>leukocytosis</u> < 15,000/mmÂ³ and serum <u>creatinine</u> < 1.5 mg/dL

* Severe CDI: <u>leukocytosis</u> â¥ 15,000/mmÂ³ or serum <u>creatinine</u> â¥ 1.5 mg/dL

* Fulminant CDI: ≥ 1 criteria of <u>severe CDI</u> plus <u>hypotension</u>, <u>shock</u>, <u>ileus</u>, and/or <u>toxic megacolon</u>





> [!TIP]
> If clinical suspicion is high, initiating <u>antibiotic</u> treatment before laboratory confirmation may be considered, especially in patients with <u>fulminant CDI</u>. [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




> [!WARNING]
> Patients with severe or fulminant disease have a higher rate of treatment failure, <u>colectomy</u>, and mortality. [[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




References: [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)

## Treatment

### General principles [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




* <u>Antibiotic</u> treatment is indicated in all symptomatic patients with <u>CDI</u> and should be guided by the <u>severity of CDI</u>.

* Asymptomatic carriers do not require <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* <u>Fecal microbiota transplantation</u> may be indicated in <u>recurrent CDI</u>, <u>severe CDI</u>, or <u>fulminant CDI</u> refractory to <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* Surgical intervention may be necessary for critically ill patients or those with complications necessitating <u>surgery</u>.

* Consultations

* Gastroenterology and/or infectious diseases in patients with insufficient treatment response or <u>recurrent CDI</u>.

* <u>Surgery</u> for critically ill patients or those with complications necessitating <u>surgery</u>

* Consider <u>intensive care unit</u> consult for patients with <u>fulminant CDI</u>. [[13]](/library/2WcTkY0)





### Supportive measures [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




* Discontinue any precipitating <u>antibiotic</u> as soon as possible.

* Correct fluid and <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances (see “<u>Initial fluids for dehydration and hypovolemia</u>” and “<u>Electrolyte repletion</u>”).

* Avoid <u>antidiarrheals</u> (e.g., <u>loperamide</u>) in patients not yet receiving <u>antibiotics</u> and those with <u>fulminant CDI</u>.





### Antibiotic therapy for CDI [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)[[3]](/library/8fcOLb0)

DOSAGE<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Recurrent CDI</u> |  | First recurrence |  | <br><br>* If the initial episode was treated with standard-dose <u>vancomycin</u>:<br><br>* Oral <u>fidaxomicin</u> DOSAGE  [[3]](/library/8fcOLb0)<br><br>* OR tapered and pulsed oral <u>vancomycin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* If the initial episode was treated with <u>metronidazole</u>: [[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)<br><br>* Oral <u>fidaxomicin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* OR standard-dose oral <u>vancomycin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |

> [!TIP]
> <u>C. difficile</u> infection is one of the rare indications for PO <u>vancomycin</u> in adults and children.




> [!WARNING]
> Intravenous administration of <u>vancomycin</u> is ineffective for <u>C. difficile</u> infection because <u>vancomycin</u> is insufficiently excreted into the <u>colon</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Consider bezlotoxumab, a <u>monoclonal antibody</u> against the <u>C. difficile</u> <u>toxin B</u>, in adults at risk of <u>recurrent CDI</u>. [[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)[[3]](/library/8fcOLb0)




### Fecal microbiota transplantation (<u>FMT</u>) [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[16]](/library/9ecNab0)




* Healthy donor stool that is administered via capsules, <u>colonoscopy</u>, or enema

* Can be considered in the following situations

* <u>Severe CDI</u> or <u>fulminant CDI</u> with insufficient clinical improvement after 48–72 hours of maximum medical therapy.  [[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)[[16]](/library/9ecNab0)

* Adult and pediatric patients with ≥ 2 recurrences despite appropriate <u>antibiotic therapy for CDI</u>  [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)





### Surgical management [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)[[2]](/library/y1cdjY0)




* Indications: critically ill patients with <u>severe CDI</u> or <u>fulminant CDI</u> refractory to <u>antibiotic therapy</u>, especially if ≥ 1 of the following are present

* Factors associated with increased mortality, e.g., severe <u>leukocytosis</u> or serum <u>lactate</u>

* Complications, e.g., <u>toxic megacolon</u>, <u>ischemia</u>, or <u>bowel perforation</u>

* Procedures

* Total <u>colectomy</u> with end <u>ileostomy</u> and stapled rectal stump

* Diverting loop <u>ileostomy</u> with <u>colonic</u> lavage followed by intraluminal <u>vancomycin</u> administration

---

## Complications

* <u>Toxic megacolon</u>

* <u>Paralytic ileus</u>

* <u>Peritonitis</u>, perforation, <u>abscess</u> formation, <u>sepsis</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prevention

### Primary <u>prevention of CDI</u>




* Judicious use of <u>antibiotics</u> and an <u>antibiotic stewardship</u> program can reduce the risk of <u>CDI</u>.

* There is insufficient evidence to recommend the discontinuation of <u>PPIs</u> or the use of probiotics to prevent <u>CDI</u>.





### Secondary prevention of CDI [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)




<u>Contact precautions</u> should be followed for all patients with suspected or diagnosed <u>CDI</u> for at least 48 hours after symptoms subside or until <u>CDI</u> is ruled out.  [[1]](/library/HiYKGK)




* Isolation: A single room with designated bathroom facilities is preferable; consider <u>patient cohorting</u> if this is not feasible.

* <u>Personal protective equipment</u>: Wear gloves and a protective gown (change after each patient); a mask is not necessary.

* <u>Hand hygiene</u>

* Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water;  before and after every patient contact (<u>C. difficile</u> spores are resistant to alcoholic <u>disinfectants</u>).

* Encourage frequent handwashing in patients with <u>CDI</u>.

* <u>Surface disinfection</u>

* Consistent <u>disinfection</u> of potentially contaminated surfaces with sporicidal oxidants (e.g., peracetic acid, <u>sodium</u> <u>hypochlorite</u>)

* During <u>outbreaks</u>, daily and <u>terminal disinfection</u> with sporicidal agents may be beneficial.

* Medical equipment

* Use disposable or dedicated equipment if possible.

* Otherwise, ensure adequate cleaning and <u>disinfection</u> that is effective against spores.

* <u>Autoclaving</u> is also sporicidal and can be used to sterilize equipment.

---

## Special patient groups

### <u>Clostridioides difficile</u> in <u>infants</u> [[17]](/library/tNcX110)[[18]](/library/FNcg110)




Most <u>infants</u> with <u>C. difficile</u> <u>colonization</u>;   are asymptomatic and do not develop <u>pseudomembranous colitis</u>.




* <u>Risk factors</u> for symptomatic disease: <u>prematurity</u> and anatomical abnormalities (e.g., <u>Hirschsprung disease</u>, <u>intestinal malrotation</u>, <u>colonic strictures</u>)

* Treatment: oral <u>vancomycin</u> or <u>metronidazole</u>
